item.title: First a Pilot, Then a Strategy: How Large Businesses are Implementing LLMs
item.description:
Over the past two years, large businesses' attitudes towards large language models have shifted. The debate about whether LLMs are needed in business has ended, and the technology has moved from being a fun toy to a strategic tool. We at Content AI conducted over 50 in-depth interviews with IT and security representatives from medium and large businesses in retail, banking, oil and gas, energy, telecom, and other sectors. The discussions covered readiness for implementation, data transfer, initiators and blockers for LLM projects, pilot economics, and vendor requirements. We will share the results and identified trends for the next 1-2 years in this article. Read more

item.title: Regression testing of prompts: An AI model acting as a reader missed three out of four texts that I edited
item.description:
I edit prompts for agents that write and check texts. To ensure that edits don't break what previously worked, I've created a set of examples with known outcomes and used it to test where an AI model acts as a reader. It was more likely to miss heavily edited texts than to flag them. The set includes two types of texts: some I later rewrote extensively by hand, others I barely touched. If a prompt edit is accepted based on such a test, defects will slip through, and the test will incorrectly pass. Read more

item.title: [Translation] No, AI Has Not Solved the Navier-Stokes Problem
item.description:
Sam Altman and other AI proponents claim AI will solve humanity's biggest problems, implying superintelligence. However, AI is merely a statistical model that reproduces trends from training data, lacking true understanding or consciousness. The current AI hype is fueled by science fiction notions of sentient machines. OpenAI's recent claim of solving the million-dollar Navier-Stokes problem is likely not a sign of machine sentience, but rather industrial espionage. The article delves into the accusations made by mathematicians Tristan Buckmaster and Einar Alpege against OpenAI, suggesting their work was stolen and plagiarized. It explores how OpenAI's data policies and model architecture might have facilitated this, and discusses the company's dire financial situation as a potential motive for such a PR stunt. The piece concludes by highlighting the ethical implications and the potential damage to the scientific community.

item.title: Tokenomics of Pricing: Three Currencies in Which We Are Billed for AI
item.description:
Beyond writing for Habr, I'm currently working on another book. AI is a great help here. It can compile materials and check facts. However, in the free version of most of them, serious work always ends the same way. Sources are analyzed, logic holds up, I finally sit down to write the final draft, and on the second paragraph, I get: 'limit exhausted, wait a few hours.' But I have time to work now. Inspiration and a complete thought in my head are also only now. All that's left is to quickly save the draft, keep the unfinished work in 'RAM,' and wait for the cooldown to end. And then start all over again. At such moments, I really want to understand what needs to be bought to avoid such breaks, and why the purchase is structured this way and not another. I promised a continuation about prices in the first text on tokenomics, and now it has a personal reason. It all comes down to computing power, not marketing. AI prices have changed more than once in a year, and there were reasons for that. Let's look at six major companies—OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot—and analyze three ways to sell AI and how they have evolved. All prices are in US dollars, as of October 1, 2026. They change often, so logic is more valuable than numbers here. Read more
